findings.title: Equal-order crypto providers are now resolved silently by classpath order, including FIPS vs default
findings.body: detectProvider now sorts by order() descending and takes the first entry. The old guard that threw 'Multiple crypto providers loaded' was removed, but no tie-breaking rule was added. DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider and WildFlyElytronProvider all return order() == 200. If two of them are on the classpath, the winner is whichever ServiceLoader lists first, with no error or warning. In a FIPS deployment where the non-FIPS default provider jar is also present, this can silently select the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider. The javadoc for order() in CryptoProvider does not say what happens on ties. Also, every discovered provider is instantiated before selection. FIPS1402Provider's constructor inserts BCFIPS and BCJSSE into the global java.security provider list and modifies security properties, so those side effects happen even when the provider is not selected. Previously this configuration failed fast.

findings.title: New abstract order() method breaks every existing CryptoProvider implementation
findings.body: order() is added as an abstract interface method with no default implementation. Any CryptoProvider implementation not updated in this PR, including out-of-tree providers and any in-repo test or helper implementations not shown in the diff, will fail to compile. A default method (for example returning 0) would keep the SPI source-compatible while still letting providers override the priority.

findings.title: Every AuthzClient.create() now requires CryptoProvider SPI discovery to succeed
findings.body: create(Configuration) now calls CryptoIntegration.init(...) unconditionally. Before this change, a plain token or HTTP client needed no crypto provider. Now, if ServiceLoader finds no CryptoProvider, init throws IllegalStateException and client construction fails even for non-ECDSA use. This can happen when the authz-client jar's META-INF/services entry is dropped by a shade or fat-jar build, or when the classloader does not expose it. Initialization is also process-wide and first-wins, so the first AuthzClient created fixes the JVM-wide provider for every other library. Consider initializing lazily only on the ECDSA signing path, or handling discovery failure.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns an unrelated JDK keystore provider, not BouncyCastle
findings.body: The method returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is typically the SUN provider for PKCS12/JKS. The CryptoProvider contract documents this method as returning the BouncyCastle provider. Any caller that uses it to register or look up the BC provider silently gets the wrong provider. The other unimplemented methods in this class throw UnsupportedOperationException, so this is also inconsistent with the class's own pattern. It should throw UnsupportedOperationException, or return the real BC provider if one is available.

findings.title: ECDSA test uses a P-256 key for ES384/ES512 and only checks a round-trip
findings.body: The key pair is always generated with the default EC size (P-256), including for the ES384 and ES512 cases. For ES512 the coordinates are then only 32 bytes, so the 66-byte coordinate path in integerToBytes is only exercised with padding and never with real P-521 values. The test also only asserts that RS -> DER -> RS is the identity. It never verifies that the DER produced by concatenatedRSToASN1DER is accepted by java.security.Signature.verify, and never checks an independently produced DER signature. A bug where both directions are wrong in a consistent way would still pass. The test should generate a curve matching each algorithm (P-256/P-384/P-521) and verify the reconstructed DER signature with the JDK verifier.

findings.title: Code appears adapted from Bouncy Castle without attribution
findings.body: The readTagNumber/readLength logic and comments, such as the quotation of X.690 8.1.2.4.2 and the 'Note: -1 will pass' comment, look taken from Bouncy Castle's ASN1InputStream. ASN1Encoder.writeLength looks similarly derived from DEROutputStream. Bouncy Castle is MIT-licensed. If this code is adapted, the source's license notice and attribution must be kept. The file header only names Red Hat copyright and @author rmartinc, which does not reflect the provenance. The author should confirm provenance and add attribution.

findings.title: No test covers the new provider selection (order precedence and ties)
findings.body: The change replaces a fail-fast policy with order-based selection and tie behavior, but no test exercises detectProvider with multiple providers, different orders, or equal orders. A unit test for precedence and tie handling would catch regressions such as the FIPS/default tie described above.
